hints: Focus on what actually changes across Period 3, the oxidation number in the highest oxide, the solubility behaviour, and the lattice type.
Write out the highest oxides: $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$, $\text{MgO}$, $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$, $\text{SiO}_2$, $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$, $\text{SO}_3$. What are the oxidation states of Na through S?
Now check water behaviour: which oxides really dissolve, which are insoluble, and which react to give acids, then match this to the bonding trend.
walkthrough:
**Check statement 1 with oxidation states**

Think of the maximum oxide for each element. Oxygen is $-2$, so the element oxidation state balances it.

$$\text{Na}_2\text{O} (+1), \text{MgO} (+2), \text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 (+3), \text{SiO}_2 (+4), \text{P}_4\text{O}_{10} (+5), \text{SO}_3 (+6)$$

**Decide if statement 1 is true**

The oxidation state rises steadily from +1 to +6 across to sulfur. It does not decrease after phosphorus, so statement 1 is false.

**Check statement 2 with water behaviour**

$\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ dissolves to give $\text{NaOH}$ and $\text{MgO}$ is only sparingly soluble, but $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ is insoluble and does not dissolve at all. $\text{SiO}_2$ is also insoluble and is not hydrolysed by water, while $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ and $\text{SO}_2$ / $\text{SO}_3$ do react with water to form acids.

$$\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 4\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$$

**Decide if statement 2 is true**

Because aluminium oxide does not dissolve and silicon dioxide does not hydrolyse, the grouping in statement 2 is wrong. So statement 2 is false.

**Check statement 3 with structure and bonding**

Across the period bonding becomes less ionic and more covalent. $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$, $\text{MgO}$, $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ are giant ionic lattices, $\text{SiO}_2$ is a giant covalent lattice, and $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$, $\text{SO}_2$, $\text{SO}_3$ are simple molecular. So statement 3 is true and only statement 3 is correct.

options.A: Incorrect because it includes statements 1 and 2. Statement 1 fails as sulfur reaches +6, higher than phosphorus (+5). Statement 2 fails as Al2O3 is insoluble and SiO2 shows no reaction with water.
options.B: Incorrect because statement 1 alone is false. Students often forget SO3 where S is +6, and think the maximum stops at P (+5). The trend is a continuous increase from Na to S.
options.C: Incorrect because statement 2 is false even though statement 3 is true. A common trap is to think all metal oxides dissolve and all non-metal oxides hydrolyse, forgetting the insoluble Al2O3 and SiO2 exceptions.
options.D: Correct because only statement 3 is true. The Period 3 oxides show the classic change: giant ionic (Na to Al) to giant covalent (Si) to simple molecular (P to S), while statements 1 and 2 contain factual errors.
